explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think so, since the verse brings David up right away. But the verse uses David as the measuring stick Ahaz doesn't match. It says, “And unlike David his father, he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD.” That one word, “unlike,” settles it.

That's the one. Verse 1 puts Ahaz next to David and then says, “And unlike David his father, he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD.” Chronicles doesn't ease into it. The first verse already tells you which way this reign is headed.
Right on the money, baker. Verse 2 says Ahaz walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and “…even made cast images of the Baals.” Notice the word “even.” It comes right before the images.

Dagon is a real name in the Bible, a god of the Philistines (Judges 16:23). But it's not the one in this verse. Ahaz makes cast images of the Baals. Easy to mix up when the Bible has a whole crowd of false gods.
Chemosh was the god of Moab (1 Kings 11:33), so you've got the right kind of name. But this verse names something else. What it says Ahaz made is cast images of the Baals.

Yes, sir. Verse 5 says the LORD delivered Ahaz into the hand of the king of Aram, who attacked him and took many captives. Chronicles says this happened to Ahaz after what the last few verses described. And Aram is only the first hit. Another one comes in the same verse.
Moab is a fair guess, baker, but it isn't mentioned in this chapter. The text says the king of Aram is the one who attacked Ahaz and took captives. Stick with what the verse names.

You're not totally off the map, because Edom does show up later in this chapter. The Edomites come and attack Judah and carry away captives (verse 17). But the one in verse 5 is the king of Aram. Right trouble, different king.
That's the one. Verse 5 says the king of Aram “…took many captives to Damascus.” Keep that name handy, because Damascus comes back later in this chapter.
Nineveh is a famous city in the Bible, so I see the pull. But it's not the city in this verse. The king of Aram takes his captives to Damascus. Big names will do that to you.
Babylon sounds like a big-name pick, and I get it. But verse 5 says the king of Aram took many captives to Damascus. Babylon is standing outside this verse with its arms crossed.

Yes, and the verse says it plainly. “For in one day Pekah son of Remaliah killed 120,000 valiant men in Judah.” Then it gives the reason: “This happened because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers.” A hundred and twenty thousand in a single day. That's a heavy verse.

The text says it straight, so True was the call here. Verse 6 says Pekah son of Remaliah killed 120,000 valiant men in Judah in one day. Then it adds, “This happened because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers.” This is one of the heavy parts of the chapter.

You got it. Verse 8 says the Israelites took the captives and a great deal of plunder and brought it to Samaria. That's also where the army is heading when a prophet walks out to meet it in the next verse.

Bethel is a real place in the Bible, but it's not on this trip. Verse 8 says the Israelites brought the captives and a great deal of plunder to Samaria. Bethel didn't make the guest list. Samaria did.
Shechem shows up in a lot of Bible stories, but not in this one. Verse 8 says the captives and the plunder go to Samaria. Sometimes the answer is just the town in the verse.

explanations.answer: Because of His wrath against Judah
explanations.explanation: That's what Oded says. “Look,” he tells them, “because of His wrath against Judah, the LORD, the God of your fathers, has delivered them into your hand.” He starts there, and notice he doesn't pat the army on the back. The very next line begins with “But.”

explanations.answer: Because Israel had stayed faithful to Him
explanations.explanation: Oded never says that. He says the LORD delivered Judah into their hand “because of His wrath against Judah…” And in the very next verse he asks the army, “But are you not also guilty before the LORD your God?” So the army isn't being praised for its faithfulness.

explanations.answer: Because Israel's army prayed before battle
explanations.explanation: The passage doesn't say a word about the army praying. Oded gives the reason himself: “because of His wrath against Judah…” When a prophet tells you why, you don't need to go looking for a different reason.

It's the opposite, and Oded doesn't whisper it. After he says the army plans to make Judah's men and women slaves, he asks, “…are you not also guilty before the LORD your God?” That question tells them they are guilty too. He doesn't clear them.

That's right. Oded says the army plans to enslave the men and women of Judah and Jerusalem, and then he asks, “…are you not also guilty before the LORD your God?” He's not giving them a pass. He's telling a whole army to look at itself.

That's what he says. “…return the captives you took from your kinsmen, for the fierce anger of the LORD is upon you.” Oded isn't asking them to think it over. He's telling them to hand the people back.
Nope, nobody's asking for the weapons back. Oded says, “…return the captives you took from your kinsmen…” The people are the point. Weapons never come up.

Chariots don't come up in Oded's speech at all. He says to “…return the captives you took from your kinsmen, for the fierce anger of the LORD is upon you.” What he cares about is the people they took.

explanations.answer: It would add to Israel's guilt before the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the reason they give. They say, “You must not bring the captives here, for you are proposing to bring guilt upon us from the LORD and to add to our sins and our guilt.” These leaders know Israel's guilt is already big, and they don't want to pile more on top.

explanations.answer: Samaria has no room to house them all
explanations.explanation: The leaders never mention room. Their reason is guilt. They say bringing the captives in would “…add to our sins and our guilt.” I think a housing problem would have been an easier excuse, and they didn't use it.

explanations.answer: Aram might come and take them back
explanations.explanation: Aram isn't part of their reasoning here. These leaders say that bringing the captives in would “…bring guilt upon us from the LORD…” The worry is about the LORD, not about anybody coming to take the captives back.
Yep. Verse 15 says they brought the captives “…to Jericho, the City of Palms, to their brothers.” Then the men returned to Samaria. Along the way they put all the feeble on donkeys.
Hebron is a real city in the Bible, but this verse doesn't name it. The men bring the captives to Jericho, the City of Palms, to their brothers. Look for the one with the palm trees.
Bethlehem has a big name in the Bible, but it's not on this trip. Verse 15 says the men took the captives to Jericho, the City of Palms. Famous place, different stop.

That's him, baker. Verse 16 says, “At that time King Ahaz sent for help from the king of Assyria.” Keep an eye on this one. Verse 20 says Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came to Ahaz but “…afflicted him rather than strengthening him.”
Egypt is a fair guess, baker, but this verse doesn't name it. Verse 16 says Ahaz sent for help from the king of Assyria. Egypt never got the call in this verse.
Babylon isn't in this part of the chapter, baker. Verse 16 says Ahaz sent for help from the king of Assyria. Babylon never even got the call.

explanations.answer: Ahaz had been most unfaithful to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. Verse 19 says the LORD humbled Judah because Ahaz “…had thrown off restraint in Judah and had been most unfaithful to the LORD.” Chronicles gives the cause right there. It doesn't leave us guessing.

explanations.answer: Judah's army had grown too proud
explanations.explanation: Chronicles never says that. It gives a different reason: Ahaz “…had been most unfaithful to the LORD.” I think pride would be an easy thing to assume, but the verse doesn't say it.

explanations.answer: Judah had refused to pay Assyria
explanations.explanation: The passage doesn't say anything about Judah refusing to pay Assyria. Verse 21 says Ahaz presented Assyria with a portion from the house of the LORD, the royal palace and the princes, and it did not help him. The reason for the humbling is in verse 19: Ahaz “…had been most unfaithful to the LORD.”
That's what the verse says. Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, came to Ahaz but “…afflicted him rather than strengthening him.” Ahaz sent for help and got hurt instead. Not what he had in mind.

I know it sounds backward, since Ahaz was the one asking for help. But verse 20 says Tiglath-pileser came to Ahaz but “…afflicted him rather than strengthening him.” So the statement was true. The help turned into the trouble.

You'd hope so, but that's not what happens. Verse 22 says, “In the time of his distress, King Ahaz became even more unfaithful to the LORD.” He didn't turn back to the LORD. He became even more unfaithful.

Right. The text says, “In the time of his distress, King Ahaz became even more unfaithful to the LORD.” Hard times can make a person turn back, but that's not what this verse says happened. Ahaz didn't turn back to the LORD.

explanations.answer: He thinks they helped Aram and might help him
explanations.explanation: That's his own reasoning. Ahaz says, “Because the gods of the kings of Aram have helped them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me.” Then the text adds, “But these gods were the downfall of Ahaz and of all Israel.” His plan didn't hold up.

explanations.answer: He wants to make peace with Aram's king
explanations.explanation: Peace with Aram isn't in the verse, baker. Ahaz gives his own reason: “Because the gods of the kings of Aram have helped them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me.” The reason he states is help, and peace isn't in it.

explanations.answer: Assyria's king orders him to do it
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say anyone orders him, baker. Ahaz states his reason: “Because the gods of the kings of Aram have helped them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me.” The text gives his reasoning and no order from Assyria's king.

That's it, baker. Verse 24 says Ahaz cut the articles of the house of God into pieces and “…shut the doors of the house of the LORD…” The place was closed up. I think this is the saddest verse in the whole chapter.
Open is the opposite of what happens. Ahaz shuts the doors of the house of the LORD. Cutting up the articles and then closing the doors is a double blow in one verse.
Repair would be a nice ending, baker, but this verse is heading the other way. Verse 24 says Ahaz cut the articles of God's house into pieces and shut its doors. I think this one is a heavy verse.

explanations.answer: On every street corner in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Exactly. Verse 24 says he “…set up altars of his own on every street corner in Jerusalem.” Every single street corner. He didn't pick one spot, he spread them across the city.

Ophel is a good-sounding pick, baker, but this verse doesn't name it. The text says Ahaz set up altars of his own on every street corner in Jerusalem. He spread them everywhere instead of picking a single spot.
Samaria is where the army went with the captives, not where Ahaz built these altars. He set them up on every street corner in Jerusalem. Different city, different story.

That's the opposite of what the verse says. Ahaz was buried in the city of Jerusalem, “…but he was not placed in the tombs of the kings of Israel.” That's how his reign ends. A king, and not even a spot with the others.

Yes, that's it. Verse 27 says Ahaz was buried in the city of Jerusalem, “…but he was not placed in the tombs of the kings of Israel.” That's a quiet end to a loud reign. And the verse ends with his son Hezekiah taking his place.
